title: Running Pace Calculator: how it works, formula and examples

content:
The [Running Pace Calculator](/running-pace-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Pace from distance and time — or time from distance and pace. Per km and per mile. Enter your what do you want to find?, distance, time and pace and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Work out your running pace from a distance and a time — or the other way round, the time a distance will take at a given pace. Pace is shown per kilometre and per mile, with average speed and the marathon time that pace would give. A 10 km run in 50 minutes is 5:00 per kilometre, 8:03 per mile and 12 km/h. Use the pace mode after a run, and the time mode before a race to see what finishing time a target pace means.

## How to use the Running Pace Calculator

Start by choosing your what do you want to find? from the list, then entering your distance (km), entering your time (minutes) and finally entering your pace (min/km). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Choose whether to find your pace or predict a time.
2. Enter the distance in kilometres.
3. Enter the time in minutes (pace mode) or the pace in minutes per kilometre (time mode).
4. Read the pace per kilometre and per mile, the speed, and the marathon equivalent.

## Formula

Pace = time ÷ distance. Time = pace × distance. Speed = distance ÷ time. 1 mile = 1.60934 km, so pace per mile = pace per km × 1.60934.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Running Pace Calculator](/running-pace-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. 10 km in 50 minutes is a pace of 5:00 per kilometre and 8:03 per mile, at an average speed of 12 km/h — and the same pace over a marathon would take 3:30:59. Try the same figures in the [Running Pace Calculator](/running-pace-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (What do you want to find?: Pace (from distance + time), Distance: 10 km, Time: 50 minutes, Pace: 5 min/km), the [Running Pace Calculator](/running-pace-calculator) returns Pace per kilometre: 5:00 min/km, Pace per mile: 8:03 min/mile, Average speed: 12 km/h, Time for a marathon (42.195 km): 3:30:59. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [BMI Calculator](/bmi-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## Pace, speed and what they feel like

Pace (minutes per kilometre) is what runners actually use, because it answers 'how long will this take?' directly. 6:00/km is a gentle jog for most people, 5:00/km is a solid club-runner pace, 4:00/km is fast, and under 3:00/km is elite. Speed in km/h is the same information upside down: 12 km/h is 5:00/km. The marathon line shows what a pace means over 42.195 km — a pace that feels easy for 5 km can be brutal for 42.

## Why the marathon time is only a guide

Multiplying your 10 km pace by 42.195 assumes you can hold the same pace for four times the distance, which almost nobody can without specific marathon training. A realistic marathon pace is usually 15–30 seconds per kilometre slower than 10 km pace. Use the line as a lower bound, then add that margin when you set a race goal.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Negative splits — a slightly slower first half — usually produce faster times than starting too fast.
- Your easy-run pace should let you hold a conversation; if you cannot, slow down.
- Compare paces on similar courses: hills and heat can cost 30 seconds per kilometre or more.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a good running pace?

For a recreational runner, 5:30–6:30 per kilometre is a normal easy pace and 5:00/km is a respectable 10 km race pace. 'Good' depends on age, distance and training — compare with your own past times first. Try it with your own numbers in the [Running Pace Calculator](/running-pace-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### How do I convert pace per km to pace per mile?

Multiply by 1.60934. A 5:00/km pace is 8:03 per mile. This calculator shows both automatically. Try it with your own numbers in the [Running Pace Calculator](/running-pace-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### How fast is 12 km/h in pace?

12 km/h is 5:00 per kilometre (60 ÷ 12). In general, pace in min/km is 60 ÷ speed in km/h. Try it with your own numbers in the [Running Pace Calculator](/running-pace-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What formula does the Running Pace Calculator use?

Pace = time ÷ distance. Time = pace × distance. Speed = distance ÷ time. 1 mile = 1.60934 km, so pace per mile = pace per km × 1.60934. You can see it in action in the [Running Pace Calculator](/running-pace-calculator) — enter your own values and the result updates as you type.
